title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 203: The Revival of Acoustic Ecology
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 203 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Revival of Acoustic Ecology

Paragraph 1. For decades, biologists counted wild animals mainly through visual methods like camera traps, binoculars, and drones. However, visual methods have serious weaknesses: creatures hide inside dense foliage, avoid human scent, or remain active only at night. Today, soundscape ecology offers a smarter approach by listening to an entire habitat's audio signature—from chirping crickets to howling monkeys—which reveals forest health far better than sight alone.

Paragraph 2. Acoustic researchers divide natural soundscapes into three parts: animal sounds, non-living weather noises such as rain, thunder, and wind, and human machine noise. In undisturbed jungles, different species evolved to call at separate sound frequencies and times so they do not block each other's signals. When humans cut down trees, this delicate acoustic balance collapses and the forest grows strangely silent.

Paragraph 3. This acoustic revolution relies on low-cost, weather-resistant recorders called ARUs attached to tree trunks. Yet a dozen recorders in one park can collect 30,000 hours of sound in a single season—far too much for humans to check manually. To solve this, Dr. Julian Rivera created SoundID software using machine learning. Instead of naming every single animal species, SoundID measures overall sound variety. In Peru, areas hit by illegal logging—which satellite photos failed to spot beneath thick leaves—showed immediate drops in sound variety within 48 hours.

Paragraph 4. Despite its success, field recording faces tough technical difficulties. High tropical humidity and tiny fungal spores slowly damage sensitive microphone parts, requiring costly repairs. Heavy monsoon downpours also drown out quiet animal calls for days, while loud highway engines near cities mask wildlife signals and trick detection software into reporting empty habitats.

Paragraph 5. Even so, sound monitoring proves vital in judging forest recovery. In Costa Rica, replanted woods looked fully grown within seven years, yet their soundscapes remained poor for nearly two decades. Specialist birds and insects only returned once fallen logs decayed and lower bushes grew back. As Dr. Bernie Krause explains, while a photograph freezes one moment, a soundscape tells the living story of an ecosystem over time.
